title: Paul McCartney’s court hearing to dissolve The Beatles’ partnership – day eleven | 1971
content:
5 March 1971 was the eleventh and final day of Paul McCartney’s court hearing to have The Beatles’ business partnership dissolved.

McCartney’s barrister, David Hirst, QC, criticised the “clever but fallacious arguments” put forward by Morris Finer, QC, the barrister of John Lennon, George Harrison, and Ringo Starr, that he said were based on “a pure forensic frolic” rather than law.

Finer suggested a compromise that would give McCartney control over his own recordings, and input in the reissuing of any Beatles material. However, the judge, Mr Justice Stamp, queried how McCartney could be expected to work with Apple in the light of the disagreements that had been heard in court over the past two weeks.

The judge then proposed that a receiver be appointed by Apple Corps and The Beatles’ business manager Allen Klein, and another by McCartney. Finer objected and proposed that there be no receiver, but that McCartney would have a representative on the board of Apple to look after his interests.

Mr Justice Stamp: Mr Finer, the position is that you are not prepared to accept my proposal, and you put forth counter ones; is that correct?

Mr Finer: With respect, yes.

Mr Justice Stamp: Mr Hirst?

Mr Hirst: Exactly the same objection, as your Lordship knows.

Mr Justice Stamp: Then I reserve my Judgment.

Mr Justice Stamp

The judge then drew a close to the proceedings, announcing that he would deliver his verdict in a week’s time. He delivered his verdict on 12 March 1971.
